## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kiṁsukopamajātaka* (Ja 248) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. Delivered by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana, the discourse was occasioned by four monks who each requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and took different approaches, prompting the Buddha to refer back to the *Kiṁsukopamasuttanta* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The canonical verse begins with the phrase *Sabbehi kiṁsuko diṭṭho* ("All have seen [the kiṁsuka]") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].
In the narrative of the past, four royal princes ask their charioteer to show them a *kiṁsuka* (Judas tree or "parrot tree") [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010]. The charioteer takes each brother separately at different times of the year: once when there is only a bare trunk, next when it exhibits young foliage, next during its flowering stage, and finally when bearing fruit [Appleton 2010]. When they subsequently discuss the tree, each describes it according to the state in which he observed it, creating confusion akin to the well-known parable of the blind men and the elephant in chapter six of the *Udāna* [Appleton 2010]. Concluding the narrative, the Buddha identifies himself as having been the King of Bārāṇasī of that time [Fausböll 1879].
SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. No cross-canonical or cross-linguistic parallels are noted by SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral], and DharmaNexus detects no cross-language matches above threshold [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus identifies internal Pali text reuse across four matching passages with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), covering 346 characters with its longest shared segment (§1.1–1.4 matching §1726–1727 at 0.94 similarity) [DharmaNexus].
